blocks.label: Introduction to complement
blocks.why: The lecturer introduces complement as a challenging but essential topic and sets expectations for the lecture.
blocks.content: Welcome to today's lecture. Today's lecture is on complement. Is anyone here familiar with the Krebs cycle? Yeah? Okay. So unfortunately, complement is like the Krebs cycle of immunology. It's really important, but it is complicated with needlessly complicated nomenclature. This is not my favorite lecture to teach. Traditionally, it is your least favorite lecture to hear about because of the really difficult nomenclature. But complement is actually a very important process, which is why we have a full lecture about it. You can just be thankful that we used to have five lectures on complement, and now we've got one lecture on complement.

blocks.label: Overview and functions of complement
blocks.why: The lecturer provides an overview of how the complement cascade is structured and outlines its primary immunological and janitorial functions.
blocks.content: Okay. So, let's start. This is an overview of complement. If you are in the natural sciences and you understand the concepts behind this one slide, then you understand enough of complement to get by. If you are in medicine, there's two slides, one at the end and this one here, that you really need to understand in order to get by. The detail does matter because it helps you understand the concepts later on, and it will certainly help you if you have an exam question on complement. But this is the key concept that you really need to be able to understand this slide. So essentially, we have, as in almost any immunological process, three different points of complement. We've got the recognition that there is a pathogen, so that complement becomes activated on it. We've got a trigger threshold because none of these things are binary. They always have to have some type of threshold at which things can start kicking into action. And then they have the effector mechanisms. And we're going to talk about the different recognition systems, then they all converge on a single trigger threshold, and then we have multiple different effector mechanisms that are triggered. Now, what complement is, in essence, is a whole set of proteins that are present and soluble in our blood, in our serum, all of the time, and they're present in this inactivated form. So our blood is full of inactivated complement, which has got these amazing properties of recognizing and destroying pathogens, but they're held in this inactive form. And the whole complement cascade is essentially understanding when you are going to activate it and then what happens after activation. Now, I'm going to skip a little bit to the end and talk about why we care about complement being activated. And the reason for this is that complement is really powerful. Once it is activated, it is able to really eradicate many different types of infections through three key processes. One of these processes is called opsonization. So opsonization is just a word that means coating a cell, a virus, coating anything, a particle, with eat me signals, so that phagocytic cells will see this particle coated with eat me signals, and they go ahead and they engulf and eat that particle. Okay? So opsonization massively enhances phagocytosis. The second thing that complement can do is it can directly lyse target cells, and we're going to talk about this later on in detail, but essentially it can punch holes in cells, and if you can punch a hole in the cell, you can kill the cell. And the third thing that complement does is it generally aids inflammation. It kick-starts many other processes. So it's an accelerant on the immune system. Now, as well as these immunological processes, it also has some janitorial roles. So it's useful for clearing away immune complexes between antibodies and antigens. It clears away apoptotic cells. If you do neuroscience, you'll find out about the role of complement in synaptic pruning. It comes up a lot of times anytime you want to dispose of something in the body. A good way to dispose of it is to coat it in complement, and then your phagocytic cells can kickstart that process of clearance.

blocks.label: Complement nomenclature
blocks.why: The lecturer explains the historical numbering conventions, cleavage fragment labeling, and nomenclature anomalies of complement proteins.
blocks.content: Now, a word on the naming. And this is important because the naming is the reason why a lot of people end up not liking complement. These are very important, so the more important something is, generally, the earlier we discovered it in immunology, and so the naming was done ages ago, and it's a bit clunky. Now, it did originally make sense. So we do have a cascade of complement that goes one, two, three, five, six, seven, eight, nine. So we do have this cascade where the numbers more or less make sense. Except they missed out, they got four in the wrong spot. Okay? So four doesn't happen after three, it happens before three, and that kind of messes it up. So we do have that that number is a little bit wrong. And generally speaking, we've got these complement forms that are all going to be cleaved, and when they get cleaved, they're in a big piece and a little piece, and generally speaking, the little piece is an A and the big piece is a B. But for complement two, they got that wrong, and it's around the other way. So these rules, they generally work, and you can probably just remember one to nine is the order of complement. And then that four is in the wrong place. So I'm sorry about that. It's just the nomenclature we got stuck with 60 years ago when people were discovering these molecules.

blocks.label: Central role and activation of C3
blocks.why: The lecturer explains why C3 serves as the central fulcrum of complement and details the biochemical actions of its cleavage products, C3a and C3b.
blocks.content: Now, the really key thing that you really should remember is complement three, because essentially what we've got is a host of upstream mechanisms, and their role is to activate complement three, C3. And then we've got a whole host of downstream mechanisms, and their job is to clear away an infection. C3 is the fulcrum of complement. And a key reaction is to go from C3, which is inactive, to cleave that and to create C3a and C3b. So those are the two active parts of complement. And then once they are active, then you can kickstart that effector process with C5 to nine. So how does C3 work? C3 is a soluble protein. It is fairly inert in its baseline state until it's going to be cut into C3a and C3b. C3b, because it's been cut, it exposes a reactive thioester bond. That bond is essentially very sticky to organic substances, so the next surface that it hits, it's going to react against and form a covalent bond, and it's going to become stuck onto that surface. Okay? Now it's such a reactive bond that if it doesn't happen quite quickly, then water will just bind it, and it will react with water, and it will become a soluble form of C3b. But for a short while, that C3b is highly sticky, and it will just covalently stick to any surface that's close by. Okay? So that's really how C3b works, is it's going to be stuck on the surface once it's activated. Now, C3a also has some key functions. C3a is quite inflammatory. It's a lot like some of these inflammatory cytokines we spoke about in earlier lectures, like TNF alpha or IL-1. It's an inflammatory molecule. So it's not just an inert product that's cut off. Both of those products have inflammatory functions.

blocks.label: The alternative pathway
blocks.why: The lecturer explains how the alternative pathway initiates spontaneously in fluid phase and amplifies on pathogen surfaces via convertases.
blocks.content: So let's go to this slide, and we're going to start by talking about the recognition. How does C3 activate on the right cells? All right. How does it activate on pathogens? And there are three separate pathways that will activate C3, called the classical pathway, the alternative pathway, and the lectin pathway. Now, the alternative pathway is the first to act and is sort of spontaneous. The lectin pathway is the second to act, typically. It is driven by the innate immune system. The classical pathway is the third to act and is driven by the adaptive immune system, although that hierarchy will be inverted on a secondary infection. If you've got an activated adaptive immune system already in place from a prior exposure, then actually the classical pathway is very, very fast.

blocks.label: Biochemical mechanism of the alternative pathway
blocks.why: It details the step-by-step activation of the alternative pathway from fluid-phase convertase formation to surface amplification.
blocks.content: So let's go through the alternative pathway first. So in a primary infection, it's the first to act. It's a very weak response because essentially it relies on the spontaneous activation of C3. So C3, like I said, it's fairly stable, but sometimes C3 at a very low rate will react with water. Now, of course, this is all happening in the blood, so water is everywhere. But at a very low rate, you get this reaction that gives you C3 bound with water. That is enough to allow a protein called factor B to bind. And once factor B is bound to C3, factor D can bind, and the function of factor D is essentially to cleave factor B. And you end up with BA, a small molecule that drifts off and doesn't do much, and factor Bb, which is a large molecule that is bound to C3. Now, this is why people hate it, because you end up with a molecule that is C3H2OBb, and you just end up having a lot of letters in there. But all this is, is C3 bound to factor B, and they've been activated. That is called the fluid phase convertase. Okay? It's a convertase because that complex is now very good at converting C3 into C3b. Yeah, it activates C3, which is what a convertase is. And it's a fluid phase because it is soluble. It's not happening down on the surface. And so this means that in any solution of blood, you're going to have a lot of inert C3, and you're going to have a very small amount of fluid phase convertase C3, which means you're going to have a very low amount of activated C3b that will be made and could potentially stick onto a pathogen if a pathogen is present. Now, you might be thinking at this point, "Well, why doesn't it stick onto our cells? Our cells are certainly present." And the answer is, it does, but we've got a host of mechanisms to clear it out quickly enough before it reaches that threshold. And we'll talk about those at the end of the lecture. Now, we've got at the top here that fluid phase convertase. So like I said in the last slide, what's essentially happening is that a very small amount of this C3 is basically an active convertase. It allows the deposition of C3b on a surface of a pathogen. Now, once it gets deposited on the surface of the pathogen, things can really kick up. So that top reaction is very slow, very weak, very easy to disrupt. Once you've got on here a C3b on the surface, that can then, again, it can bind factor B, factor B can recruit factor D, factor D activates B, and that's exactly the same as what happened above. You're getting the same convertase complex, but this is not a fluid phase convertase, this is a surface convertase because it's bound to that surface. And the critical thing here is that now you're going to have that same reaction occur over and over again in a concentrated location. So rather than having one molecule bump around in the blood and disperse and be inactivated, one molecule will create two molecules, which will create 10 molecules, which will create 100 molecules, very concentrated, so that the processes which downregulate and destroy complement activation, they're not going to be fast enough, and it's going to catalyze and reach a critical mass. Okay? Because at this point, you can just create a whole ton of C3b on the surface. You're going to get a whole ton of convertases. Everything gets kickstarted. So that's the alternative pathway.

blocks.label: The lectin pathway
blocks.why: The lecturer describes the lectin pathway and how mannose-binding lectin triggers convertase formation on bacterial surfaces.
blocks.content: Now, if we go to the lectin pathway, the lectin pathway is essentially the link between the innate immune system and complement. This is activated by a couple of different proteins. The most important of these is mannose-binding lectin. Mannose-binding lectin is essentially a pattern recognition receptor. Okay? It's a soluble pattern recognition receptor, so it's not expressed inside a cell or on the surface of the cell. It's just expressed, and it's floating around in the blood. But what it does is it binds mannose and fucose residues. These are residues that are really quite rare in vertebrate cells. They're quite common in bacterial cells. And so, you are able to enrich the activation, the binding of mannose-binding lectin onto bacterial surfaces. Now, mannose-binding lectin, once it's present, it's going to bind C4. So this is the one that is in the wrong order. And C4, once it's bound, acts in a very similar way to C3. Okay? So C4, if it's bound to mannose-binding lectin, it creates a reactive bond that sticks onto the surface. It gets cut into C4a, C4b. The C4b is the important part that's stuck on the surface. Now we have complement two coming in. Complement two gets cleaved. Here, again, complement two is the odd one of the naming in that C2a is the big bit that sticks on while C2b floats off. But that gives you this complex of C4bC2a. C4bC2a can bind C3 and will act as a convertase. This is the classical convertase because it's the same convertase that is generated in the classical pathway for complement activation. So that's C4bC2a, and that convertase is going to now start producing a whole bunch of C3b deposit on the surface. So again, you've reached a surface-bound convertase. You can put a ton of C3b onto that surface. It's concentrated so that the systems that normally dissipate complement, they get overwhelmed, and you're getting a reaction that is going.

blocks.label: The classical pathway
blocks.why: The lecturer explains how the classical pathway activates complement through antibody binding and C1 recruitment.
blocks.content: Now, the third pathway to recognize a pathogen by complement is the classical pathway. This pathway is linked to antibodies. I know you haven't really learned about antibodies yet in detail. That will be in the next few lectures. But I think at this moment, it's sufficient just to say that you've got antibodies, you've got two ends. You've got an end that sticks to pathogens, and then you've got a constant region. That end that sticks to pathogens is different for every antibody. The constant region is the same for every antibody. And when the antibody is bound to the surface, we have that constant region gets bound by C1, and C1 kickstarts this process. It allows C4 to bind. C4 gets activated, C2 binds. That complex is the classical convertase, and that classical convertase ends up creating a whole bunch of C3b bound onto the surface.

blocks.label: Threshold and synergy in complement activation
blocks.why: The lecturer explains how multiple activation pathways converge and require a local concentration to surpass the activation threshold.
blocks.content: So we've got three different mechanisms by which C3 can start being deposited on the surface. These mechanisms can, of course, synergize. You can have a little bit of mannose-binding lectin and a little bit of antibody, and they're going to synergize quite nicely because all that matters is that you're getting C3 on the surface. You've got these processes that will clear C3 off of the surface, and essentially, it's all about, are you putting down complement faster than the rate at which it's being cleared? And if you aren't, then the reaction just dies off. Nothing happens. If you are putting down complement faster than the clearance, then you're going to reach the trigger threshold, where you've got a local concentration of activated C3 convertase, and that allows All the effector molecules to start happening. Okay? So that's really critical to understand that this trigger threshold, it doesn't happen from one molecule of complement being activated. You really need to have a local concentration of complement. Now, that trigger threshold, I said here, this is that key reaction again where C3 has to bind, and it's really about the amount of C3b that is bound in a concentrated location.

blocks.label: Effector mechanism: opsonization
blocks.why: The lecturer explains how complement facilitates opsonization and phagocytosis through C3b and C5a signaling.
blocks.content: So how about the effector functions? So I mentioned at the start there's opsonization, inflammation, and lysis of pathogens. Let's go first to the opsonization. So opsonization, this is the eat me signal that I was mentioning, and this is because C3b is directly recognized by phagocytes. Phagocytes have got a couple of key complement receptors, in particular, complement receptor one and complement receptor three. They're going to see C3b on a surface, and that will allow them to bind. So now they've got a target to eat that pathogen. They also need to get a second signal, though, to actually finish up the eating, and the second signal is the exposure of C5a through this C5 receptor. So C5a is one of the molecules we'll talk about in a second. It's a byproduct of complement activation. So if you have complement activation, you're going to get some C5a made, and that would then tell the phagocyte that it can go and eat that complement-bound pathogen.

blocks.label: Effector mechanism: inflammation
blocks.why: The lecturer describes how C3a acts as a soluble inflammatory mediator to recruit other immune cells.
blocks.content: Now, the second part is this generic inflammation, and I mentioned here that this is the function of C3a, so the bit that gets cut off and doesn't bind, that floats around and is an inflammatory mediator. It drives the recruitment of other cells. It's very non-specific. It's not going to target this particular pathogen. It'll just get other cells into the right site and responsive.

blocks.label: Effector mechanism: membrane attack complex and lysis
blocks.why: The lecturer explains how the membrane attack complex forms pores to lyse gram-negative bacteria and enveloped viruses.
blocks.content: And then the third pathway is that of lysis of the pathogen. And this is the activation of the membrane attack complex. So the membrane attack complex happens when we have got this, a lot of C3b on the surface. Now, C3b can be part of a C3 convertase, but it can also form a C5 convertase. It forms a C5 convertase by having two molecules of C3b stuck together with that factor B, large part B, and that will then bind. That is the C5 convertase. What C5 convertase does is it cuts C5 in half. So you've now got C5 being cut into C5a, C5b. C5a floats off and is this general inflammatory signal, same as C3a. In a lot of ways, C5 is very similar to C3. The C5b, that doesn't directly bind the surface of the pathogen. Instead, it binds C6 and seven, and then that allows it to be embedded onto the surface. That would then recruit C8. C8 starts to recruit C9, and so we've now got the numbering where it all makes sense, right? So five recruits six, seven, eight, nine. You get multiple C9s being recruited, and that forms this pore. The more and more C9 that goes into that complex, the bigger that pore grows, and you end up with what is essentially a large hole in the membrane. Now, this is quite effective against gram-negative bacteria in particular, and enveloped viruses. Does anyone want to guess why it's not very effective against gram-positive bacteria? I'm going to say after that, I think it might be because they don't have a cell wall. Exactly, yeah. Gram-positive bacteria have a very thick cell wall, and so if the complement is being deposited on the outside of that cell wall, the C9 doesn't actually reach down into the membrane, and so it doesn't lyse the membrane. So the membrane attack complex doesn't work particularly well against gram-positive bacteria. And the same is true against non-enveloped viruses. If that virus is just a protein capsid, you can still have the phagocytic functions saying, "Eat me," but you're not going to get the membrane attack complex do anything useful because there is no membrane to attack.

blocks.label: Regulation of complement and host cell protection
blocks.why: The lecturer details the regulatory proteins that protect host cells from accidental complement activation and lysis.
blocks.content: So that's how complement works. That's how complement destroys bacteria and viruses. And then this brings up the question of why isn't it destroying our own cells? And this is because it is highly regulated. I've said a few times that just a couple of molecules of complement doesn't give you activation because there are these systems to clear it away. Now, most of the regulators are negative regulators that shut it down. This is the only regulator that's a positive factor, a positive helper. This is properdin. It's not particularly important from your perspective. I only mention it because just to say that there are positive regulators, and this is it. The other regulators are all negative regulators, and this is really what's quite important because we need to make sure the complement doesn't kill our own cells. Now, the key negative regulator is factor I, I as in inhibitor. It inhibits this complex. In fact, it can cleave C3b to inactivate it. So it makes inactivated C3b, just makes that completely inert. Now, it needs to work in conjunction with another factor, so either MCP or Factor H. So here's how it works in conjunction with MCP, membrane cofactor protein. What is happening now is that the host cell, our cells, are covered with MCP. We've got lots of this MCP on our surface. And essentially, if we get some complement accidentally deposited on our cell, MCP will bind the C3b. Once it's bound, it boots off factor Bb, which makes the complement inert, and then factor I binds instead, and it cleaves the C3b. Okay, so it inactivates that C3b. And this is happening all the time because our cells are coated with MCP, and we've always got a little bit of activational complement happening, so always a little bit of complement being deposited, and then it's being inactivated by MCP and factor I. Factor H is working in a very similar way. So Factor H is quite similar to MCP in that it coats all of our cells. It's actually a soluble protein. It's not a protein produced by our cells as a transmembrane protein. It's a soluble protein, but it binds sialic acid. And we've got a lot of sialic acid on the surface of our cells. So all of that sialic acid on the surface of our cells binds Factor H. So in effect, we've got a ton of Factor H on the surface of our cells. That Factor H is going to bind any of that C3 convertase, the C3bbbb. And it boots off the Bb and allows Factor I to bind. And again, once Factor I is bind, it can inactivate, it can cleave C3b. So this is a system that either MCP or Factor H, in effect, what they do is they recruit Factor I, Factor I cuts off the C3 convertase, and it shuts that reaction down permanently. There is another protein called decay accelerating factor. Again, it's present on the surface of our cells at quite high levels. And what the decay accelerating factor does is it just boots off Bb, which makes the C3b inert. It doesn't recruit Factor I, though, so it doesn't permanently inactivate it. It just slows the reaction down. But you can see how important it is for us to not have complement attacking our surfaces because we've got these three different systems that are all present, that are all shutting down any complement that is being activated on the surface of our cells. And then the final regulatory protein to talk about is a protein called protectin. Now, the other proteins were all based on trying to make sure we don't get complement three activated on the surface of our cells. What protectin does is it prevents the insertion of 5b-6-7-8. And 5b-6-7-8 is that complex that can get into the membrane and start the recruitment of complement nine. It builds the membrane attack pore, and that is disrupted by protectin. So together, these different factors, MCP, decay accelerating factor, Factor H, protectin, they're going to prevent complement from damaging the host cell. Now, this system can be overwhelmed. What this is good at is it raises the threshold for C3 locally. But if you were to do something like throw some antibodies on this cell and then have complement on those antibodies, then that's going to give you quite a powerful convertase that can overwhelm these protection systems. So these protection systems are really good at stopping the spontaneous activation of complement, but they are not enough to overcome the directed activation of complement by antibodies in the classical pathway.

blocks.label: Clinical complement deficiencies
blocks.why: The lecturer analyzes how deficiencies in different complement components result in distinct clinical manifestations.
blocks.content: Now, I mentioned at the start that for med students here, there are two critical slides. That first slide, this is the second critical slide. So this is the reason why you have to really care about complement, because complement deficiency is one of the most important clinical deficiencies in the immune system that you'll see. It's pretty common to have patients that are deficient in a complement pathway member, either because of a genetic deficiency in one of the genes that produces these or an induced deficiency where the complement is not being made at high enough levels, so the levels drop in the blood and you get a secondary deficiency of complement. Now, it'd be nice to be able to say if you have a deficiency in complement, you have more infections and leave it at that. But actually, the different molecules of complement end up having different clinical presentations, sometimes quite different clinical presentations, which is why it's important for you to know how the pathway works, so you can understand why a C3 deficiency is very different from a Factor I deficiency, for example. So let's just go over these deficiencies. If you have a deficiency in C1, C2, or C4, these are the upstream molecules. These are the molecules that are initiating C3 activation on the surface. You have a propensity to infection because you're not very good at activating complement, but you also have an issue with clearing away immunoglobulin, because some of this function of C1, for example, is to clear away immunoglobulin, so the complexes end up being highly present. You don't get rid of them. They start depositing in places like the joints. You can get arthritis. You can get deposition in the kidney. You can get nephritis. They are correlated with things like lupus development. So you get these two different sets of symptoms because you're not clearing away the immune complexes and you're not making complement activate very well. Now, if you've got a deficiency in C3, that's quite simple. The whole complement pathway depends on C3, so you're going to have an issue with infections, and in particular, you get an issue with encapsulated bacteria, pyrogenic bacteria. If you have a deficiency in C5 to C9, that is less severe because that's just the membrane attack complex. You still have the eat me signals, but you're not producing this membrane attack complex, and it ends up that clinically what you see is mostly Neisseria infections. A deficiency in Factor D or properdin, these are sort of weaker parts of the pathway, so you tend to see pyrogenic bacteria and Neisseria infections. Now, Factor I and Factor H, these are opposites. So these are the inhibitors of the pathway. And you would think that if you had a loss of the inhibitors, you should have a more activated complement system, and you're going to be able to get rid of bacteria more easily. And that's true, you do have a more activated complement system, but actually, the complement system becomes so much more activated that you end up just using up all the C3. So in effect, you have an issue with not being able to shut down complement, and that gives you a secondary deficiency in complement three, so you get this deficiency in immunity, and you get pyrogenic bacteria the same way you do if you have a C3 deficiency. And then finally, if you have a deficiency in decay accelerating factor or protectin, these are the factors that protect our cells from being killed off by complement, and so you end up with a disease that is very autoimmune-like because complement that does get activated on our cells is able to create membrane attack complexes and is able to kill off our cells. So you end up having a very different presentation that's all about autoimmune-like symptoms rather than infection symptoms. So this is very important for clinical students to learn and understand this slide, and I'm sorry, but it does mean learning the pathway enough to be able to remember why these different molecules have different functions in their deficiencies.

blocks.label: Pathogen evasion of complement
blocks.why: The lecturer discusses how pathogens evade complement, focusing on Staphylococcus aureus mechanisms and laboratory uses of protein A.
blocks.content: Now, the other thing that's quite interesting about complement, and it's a sign of how important it is, is the evasion strategies that have been developed by different infections. And the fact that it's so powerful gives a large selective pressure on pathogens to be able to evade complement. Now, when I talk about evasion, I don't mean perfect evasion. I mean just being able to reduce the speed at which complement gets rid of these pathogens. And in a way, it is the defining feature of a pathogen as opposed to a commensal that it can get past some of the complement strategies, and at least live with complement for a short amount of time before the complement builds up to too high a level and kills off the pathogen. There are multiple different evasion mechanisms that have been evolved multiple times in evolutionarily independent processes, which again show how important complement is, because pathogens have made many different ways to evade the complement. Now, these can involve interfering between the binding of antibody and complement. You can bind and inactivate the complement components. You can destroy complement components with a protease, and you can mimic inhibitory regulators that basically act like a host inhibitor so that the bacterial cell can become invisible the same way that our vertebrate cells are. And we're really just going to give one example here, which is Staphylococcus aureus. So this Staphylococcus is, in its baseline state, highly sensitive to complement, so it has evolved multiple different mechanisms in order to be able to partially evade complement. Now, these include having a cell wall that is protected by a polysaccharide capsule. That capsule is constantly being made, constantly being shed. Now, that means that any convertase that is being bound on the surface of that capsule doesn't stay there for that long. Eat me signals are being diluted because it's constantly shedding its capsule. Yeah, it's like having a reptile shed its skin all the time to get rid of anything that's bound on it. They also have a protein called Staphylococcus complement inhibitor, Scn, which is actively preventing the generation of C3b bound to the surface. They secrete multiple different proteins that will bind, degrade, and inactivate C3, and so actually what they can do is cause a local C3 deficiency. They have a factor called clumping factor A, and so clumping factor A recruits factor I to the bacterial surface. So in effect, clumping factor A is like sialic acid on our cells. It is a signal that recruits factor I saying, "No, no, this is a safe cell. We shouldn't be activating complement three on this surface. We've got all this factor I to inactivate it." So it's using the host inactivation system to inactivate complement by mimicking the effect of something like sialic acid. Then we've got chemotaxis inhibitory protein. This blocks the C5a chemotactic receptor on neutrophils, and so essentially it just blocks that one particular product of C5a, which would be recruiting neutrophils. And then finally, we've got this protein, staphylococcal protein A. And what protein A does is it binds antibodies in the same place where the antibodies would kickstart complement reaction by binding C1q. Now, that means that the antibodies are essentially capped and they can't recruit complement, and so that shuts down that classical pathway, or at least it slows down the classical pathway of complement activation. Now, we actually use protein A by Staphylococcus in a few different purposes. So clinically, if you've got a serum that you want to transfer into a patient and you don't want to transfer over the antibodies, so you want to transfer serum but purge that serum of antibodies, you will use factor A to soak up-- Sorry, you'll use protein A to soak up all those antibodies and just give you nice clean serum that doesn't have antibodies anymore that can be transferred into a patient. We also use it in the lab quite a lot where we want to purify antibodies. And so there what we'll do is we'll take a column, the column will be bound to protein A. We'll run serum over that column. We'll collect up all the protein, the immunoglobulin, the antibody on the column bound to the protein A. Everything else flows off, and then we can elute afterwards with acid, the antibodies. So there are really useful medical and laboratory functions for protein A that we're able to take advantage of, all because this bacteria has evolved systems to circumvent complement.

blocks.label: Closing and next lecture preview
blocks.why: The lecturer concludes the lecture and previews the upcoming topic on the adaptive immune system.
blocks.content: Okay. So I think, with that, we can finish up with complement. This is the end of my first set of lecture series, and the next lecture is the adaptive immune system. Thank you.
